```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(lactater)
library(dplyr)
```

lactater turns the stages of a step test into lactate thresholds, checks them, and puts them to use. Find what you want
to do, and the function that does it:

```{r tasks, echo = FALSE, eval = requireNamespace("gt", quietly = TRUE)}
site <- "https://fmmattioni.github.io/lactater/articles/"
tasks <- tibble::tribble(
  ~step, ~task, ~functions, ~article,
  "Before the test", "Record every test the same way", "The web form, `read_recording()`, `recording_sheet()`",
  "best-practices|Best practices",
  "Analyze it", "Estimate every threshold", "`lactate_threshold()`", "methods|The methods and the evidence",
  "Analyze it", "See how the methods agree", "`autoplot()`", "",
  "Analyze it", "Check the data and the curve", "`lactate_checks()`, `lactate_diagnostics()`",
  "checking|Checking the analysis",
  "Analyze it", "Know how sure each threshold is", "`ci = TRUE`", "checking|Checking the analysis",
  "Use it", "Build three or five training zones", "`lactate_zones()`", "zones|Training zones",
  "Use it", "Count the training in each zone", "`training_load()`", "training-load|Training load",
  "Use it", "Predict race performance", "`predict_performance()`, `calibrate_performance()`",
  "performance|Predicting performance",
  "Use it", "Compare two tests, or follow a series", "`compare_tests()`, `curve_shape()`, `lactate_trend()`",
  "compare|Comparing tests",
  "Use it", "Compare with the population of the same age and sex", "`reference_percentiles()`",
  "compare|Comparing tests",
  "Share it", "Report the test to an athlete or a coach", "`test_report()`", "",
  "Share it", "A table for a paper", "`lactate_report()`", ""
)
parts <- strsplit(tasks$article, "|", fixed = TRUE)
tasks$article <- vapply(parts, function(p) if (length(p) == 2) sprintf("[%s](%s%s.html)", p[2], site, p[1]) else "", "")
gt::gt(tasks, groupname_col = "step") |>
  gt::fmt_markdown(columns = c("functions", "article")) |>
  gt::cols_label(task = "You want to", functions = "Use", article = "Read more") |>
  gt::cols_width(task ~ gt::pct(36), functions ~ gt::pct(38), article ~ gt::pct(26)) |>
  gt_lactater()
```

## Your data

One row per stage of a step test: the intensity (power in W, or speed), the lactate measured at the end of the
stage and, if you have them, the heart rate and the rating of perceived exertion (RPE). A resting sample, if you took
one, is the row with intensity 0.

```{r}
demo_data
```

Your own test comes in with `read.csv("test.csv")` in those columns, or with `read_recording()` from the .xlsx of
the [web form](https://fmmattioni.github.io/lactater/step-test-form.html). Rows with a missing lactate (a missed
sample) are dropped with a warning. If the last stage was not completed, enter its time-weighted intensity (as
`demo_data` does for its 2-min last stage at 191 W), or leave it out with `max_intensity`. How to collect data that does the methods justice is in [Best practices for a step
test](https://fmmattioni.github.io/lactater/articles/best-practices.html).

## Estimate the thresholds

```{r}
results <- lactate_threshold(
  demo_data,
  intensity_column = intensity,
  lactate_column = lactate,
  heart_rate_column = heart_rate,
  rpe_column = rpe,
  plot = FALSE
)
results
```

The column arguments can also go by position, as in the calls below: `lactate_threshold(demo_data, intensity,
lactate, heart_rate)`. Every method runs by default; pick some with `method`, e.g. `method = c("Dmax", "LTP")`, and
set `sport` for running, swimming or rowing. `rpe_column` gives the RPE at each threshold (add `rpe_scale = "CR10"`
for the 0-10 scale; the RPE of `demo_data` is simulated).

Two of these thresholds are what training needs. LT1 is the first rise of lactate above resting values, the top of
the moderate intensity domain; LT2 is the second, abrupt rise, the top of the heavy domain. The methods aim at one of
them or at a fixed lactate value, the three categories of [Faude et al. (2009)](https://doi.org/10.2165/00007256-200939060-00003): the first rise (Log-log, Bsln + 0.5 and 1.0,
LT<sub>ratio</sub>, LTP1), the second rise or the maximal lactate steady state (Bsln + 1.5, the D<sub>max</sub> family,
LTP2, IAT, Stegmann), and fixed values (OBLA). `autoplot()` groups them this way, and [The methods and the evidence](https://fmmattioni.github.io/lactater/articles/methods.html) says
which to trust. A threshold is `NA` when its method found nothing in the tested range: the Log-log lines crossing
outside the stages, a D<sub>max</sub> curve never below its line, LTP2 in a test that stopped early.
`lactate_checks()` names them and says what to do.

## Look at them

The overview puts every threshold on the same intensity axis as the curve, one row per method, with a table of the
values at each threshold:

```{r, fig.height = 7.5, fig.width = 8}
autoplot(results)
```

Or look at one method in detail:

```{r}
autoplot(results, method = "ModDmax")
```

## Check the analysis

`lactate_checks()` flags what is easy to miss in a table of numbers, and `lactate_diagnostics()` checks the fitted
curve and how much each threshold rests on single stages:

```{r}
lactate_checks(results)
diagnostics <- lactate_diagnostics(results)
diagnostics
```

```{r, fig.height = 11, fig.width = 9}
autoplot(diagnostics)
```

## How sure are we?

With 6 to 10 stages, a threshold reported to 0.1 W is false precision. `ci = TRUE` adds bootstrap confidence
intervals (this takes a few seconds; use more replicates than this for real work):

```{r}
set.seed(2024)
with_ci <- demo_data |>
  lactate_threshold(
    intensity, lactate, heart_rate,
    method = c("OBLA", "Dmax", "LTP"), plot = FALSE, ci = TRUE, n_boot = 200
  )

with_ci |>
  select(method, intensity, intensity_low, intensity_high)
```

## Training zones

By default LT1 is Bsln + 0.5 and LT2 Log-Poly-ModD<sub>max</sub>, the pair with the best evidence for each boundary
([Training zones](https://fmmattioni.github.io/lactater/articles/zones.html) says why); choose others with `lt1` and
`lt2`, and three or five zones with `model`:

```{r, fig.height = 6.5}
zones <- lactate_zones(results, model = 5)
zones
autoplot(zones)
```

## A table for your report

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("gt", quietly = TRUE)}
lactate_report(results)
```

For the athlete or the coach, `test_report()` writes the whole test as one web page (and PDF): their details, LT1 and
LT2, the zones, every threshold, the predicted performance, the checks and the stages (see [a
cyclist](https://fmmattioni.github.io/lactater/report-example.html) and [a
runner](https://fmmattioni.github.io/lactater/report-running-example.html)). Give it two to five tests of one athlete
and their `dates`, and it reports the progress over them ([see an
example](https://fmmattioni.github.io/lactater/report-series-example.html)).

## Many tests at once

Use `.by` with the columns that identify each test. `lactate_tests` holds 16 tests across sports and fitness levels;
here, the six tests of one cyclist:

```{r}
lactate_tests |>
  filter(athlete == "cyclist_series") |>
  lactate_threshold(intensity, lactate, method = "Dmax", dmax_methods = "ModDmax", plot = FALSE, .by = "day")
```

## Learn more

* [Best practices for a step test](https://fmmattioni.github.io/lactater/articles/best-practices.html): how to run
  a test, as a checklist with sources.
* [The methods and the evidence](https://fmmattioni.github.io/lactater/articles/methods.html): how each method is
  defined and what the evidence says.
* [Checking the analysis](https://fmmattioni.github.io/lactater/articles/checking.html): checks, regression
  diagnostics, and bootstrap intervals.
* [Training zones](https://fmmattioni.github.io/lactater/articles/zones.html): choosing LT1 and LT2, three and five
  zones.
* [Training load](https://fmmattioni.github.io/lactater/articles/training-load.html): time in zone and intensity
  distribution.
* [Comparing tests](https://fmmattioni.github.io/lactater/articles/compare.html): is a change real, did the curve
  shift or change shape, and trends.
* [Predicting performance](https://fmmattioni.github.io/lactater/articles/performance.html): race times from a step
  test, how sure they are, and your own equation.
* [Beyond the step test](https://fmmattioni.github.io/lactater/articles/beyond-the-step-test.html): the maximal lactate
  steady state from constant-load bouts, and the maximal lactate accumulation rate (V̇La<sub>max</sub>) from a sprint test.
* [The example data](https://fmmattioni.github.io/lactater/articles/example-data.html): 16 tests across sports.
